doc.title: Christian McBride interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Last-minute solo bass on Night Train and Little Sunflower
summary: He put off arranging his solo bass feature, devised Night Train in twenty minutes and did three takes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Really. You’ve got “Night Train” on there and I said all right, “Night Train.” A classic blues thing. I was wondering, like how is he going to do this? And it’s just bass, right?

Yeah. Every time I think about how I did it I get tired. Because I did the same thing on the new album as I did on “Getting To It.” The producer said, “Well you know why don’t you feature yourself on something, you know, just unaccompanied bass?” I said well sometimes — this is not a good habit — sometimes it works out and sometimes it doesn’t, but I tend to wait until the last minute to do some things. So things get so backed up and sometimes I don’t get to things until the last minute. So I didn’t really think of an arrangement for myself until maybe two days before I was supposed to go into the studio. So the producers kept saying, you know, “What do you got, what do you got?” I said, “Uhhh, it’s a surprise, I’ll tell you.” So come the day of the session — oh I remember how it happened — getting to it took three days. So we figured we would knock all of the ensemble stuff out on the first two days and I’d do my solo piece and the stuff with Ray Brown and Milt Hinton on the last day. The session went so smoothly, the bulk of the album was finished after the first day.

Right. So they said, “Well look, Christian you have all this time, why don’t you do your solo now?” I said, “Uhhh, can I wait, please?” They said, “No, why don’t you do it today?” I said, “Okay.” So I took my bass in the back and I said, “Give me about twenty minutes.” So I figured out this arrangement of “Night Train” on the spur of the moment. And it really takes a lot of energy. I really backed myself up into a jam because sometimes people, like you know they ask me to play it in person. That takes a lot of energy, man.
How many takes did it take you?

I did three takes. Yeah. I had my heart beating fast and I was sweating and carrying on. And the same thing happened on the new album when I did “Little Sunflower” because you know, once again they said, “What’s your bass feature going to be?” I said, “Ohhh, you’ll see.” But once again it worked out.
